title: Turkey and Egypt Sign Defense Industry MoU in Sarajevo as Ankara Courts Cairo for the Mecca Pact; Lira Hot-Money Boom Hits $75B
subhead: Ankara deepens defense-industrial ties with Cairo outside the trilateral Mecca Pact framework, while a surge of foreign capital into lira assets forces policymakers to weigh curbing speculative inflows. Erdogan also sharpened warnings to Greece over Aegean island militarization.

sections.heading: Turkey-Egypt Defense MoU Signed in Sarajevo
sections.body:
Turkey and Egypt signed a memorandum of understanding to expand defense industry cooperation on Wednesday on the sidelines of the First Balkan Shield Defence Industry Exhibition and Summit in Sarajevo, according to Al Bawaba. The deal was signed by Egyptian defense companies affiliated with the Ministry of Military Production and Turkey's state-owned Mechanical and Chemical Industry Corporation (MKE), in the presence of Egypt's Minister of State for Military Production Salah Soliman Gomblat and Turkey's Deputy Defence Minister Salih Ayhan.

Gomblat framed the agreement as part of President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's push for strategic partnerships, citing opportunities for industrial partnerships and technical exchange. Ayhan said Turkey was seeking to strengthen defense cooperation with friendly countries. The MoU gives Cairo a separate channel for defense cooperation with Ankara without formally joining the trilateral Saudi-Turkish-Pakistani Mecca Pact, which Egypt has so far declined to sign despite participating in earlier 'quad' consultations.
sections.whyItMatters: The MoU is a concrete step in the Turkey-Egypt rapprochement and signals Ankara's strategy of building defense ties with Cairo incrementally, even as Egypt keeps its distance from the Mecca Pact's binding collective-defense clause.

sections.heading: Ankara's Push to Bring Egypt Into the Mecca Pact
sections.body:
Middle East Monitor analysis details why Turkey wants Egypt inside the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed August 7 by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan. Egypt would bring substantial military capacity, control of the Suez Canal, and a presence in both the Mediterranean and Red Sea, extending the pact's reach across major energy and commercial routes. Its membership would also turn the informal four-country consultations into a more coherent framework.

The energy logic is clear: Egypt's Idku and Damietta LNG liquefaction plants are the Eastern Mediterranean's only large-scale export facilities, complementing Turkey's pipelines, storage and regasification capacity. Cairo, however, remains cautious — Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said Egypt is studying accession 'very seriously,' but a binding defense obligation could complicate its peace treaty with Israel and its role as a mediator. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has called Egypt a natural partner and suggested it could join later once technical questions are resolved.
sections.whyItMatters: Egypt's membership would transform the Mecca Pact from a trilateral arrangement into a broader framework linking the Gulf, Eastern Mediterranean and Red Sea — but Cairo's caution reflects the real constraints of binding defense commitments in a volatile region.

sections.heading: Lira Hot-Money Boom Creates Policymaker Dilemma
sections.body:
Bloomberg reports a surge of money into Turkish lira assets — a $75 billion hot-money boom — is creating a dilemma for policymakers weighing how to curb speculative inflows. The influx has helped stabilize the currency and economy, but carries the risk of sudden reversals that could destabilize markets.

Separately, MSN economics coverage notes Turkey's economy has stabilized enough to return $5 billion previously borrowed from Saudi Arabia, helped by sharply higher reserves. The repayment is a sign of improved external finances after years of reserve depletion and currency pressure. The hot-money dynamic puts the central bank in a bind: welcoming inflows supports the lira and reserves, but the speculative, short-term nature of the capital leaves Turkey exposed if global conditions shift.
sections.whyItMatters: The capital inflow is a vote of confidence in Turkey's post-election economic stabilization, but the speculative character of the money means policymakers must balance short-term currency support against the risk of a disruptive outflow.

sections.heading: Erdogan Sharpens Warnings to Greece Over Aegean Islands
sections.body:
President Erdogan, speaking to journalists on the flight home from the SCO summit in Kyrgyzstan, told Greece to 'turn back from the wrong path' and halt the militarization of Aegean islands that Ankara considers bound by demilitarized status, according to Greek City Times. Asked what Turkey would do if the arming continued, he said Ankara would 'do what is necessary,' and warned that anyone reading Turkey's 'calm and prudent approach' as weakness is making a 'grave mistake.'

The comments follow Greece's $3.2 billion air defense deal with Israel and Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis's line that regional defense plans will not change despite Turkish objections. Turkey's legal case rests on the 1923 Treaty of Lausanne and the 1947 Paris Peace Treaty, which Ankara says placed eastern Aegean islands and the Dodecanese under a demilitarized regime. Greece rejects that reading, arguing self-defense is non-negotiable. In late August, Turkey's Defense Ministry objected to reported UAV activity on Rhodes while calling Greece's relocation of Patriot batteries from Karpathos to Crete a 'positive step.'
sections.whyItMatters: Erdogan's remarks restate a standing Turkish red line rather than announcing a new operational step, but the timing — after the Greece-Israel defense deal — signals Ankara is watching Athens' military buildup closely and will not let it pass without public pushback.

sections.heading: Israel-Turkey Backchannel Dries Up as Syria Rivalry Simmers
sections.body:
Ynet reports that Azerbaijan-mediated backchannel contacts between Israel and Turkey have declined as tensions rise, with a senior Israeli official saying the channel has effectively dried up. The deterioration follows Israel's August 18 strike on the Abu al-Duhur airbase in northern Syria, which Israel said was meant to stop Turkey from deploying air-defense systems there — a claim Ankara denied.

Middle East Institute Syria expert Charles Lister told i24NEWS that informal security arrangements governing Israeli and Turkish military activity in Syria have effectively broken down since the strike. Those arrangements, reportedly reached through talks in Baku, included separate areas of operation and a direct hotline to prevent accidental confrontation. Lister said the strike, far north of the understood dividing line near the T4 airbase, surprised US officials and created the impression Israel was trying to move the boundary closer to Turkey. He warned that without renewed diplomatic engagement, the risk of escalation increases, though neither side appears to want direct conflict.
sections.whyItMatters: The collapse of the informal deconfliction mechanism in Syria removes a key safeguard against accidental Israel-Turkey confrontation, and the US appears eager to restore it — but the Abu al-Duhur strike has eroded trust on both sides.

sections.heading: Black Sea Grain Plan Stalls as Russia Rules Out Reviving Old Deal
sections.body:
Russia's Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko said Wednesday there are no grounds to revive the 2022 Black Sea grain initiative, from which Moscow withdrew in 2023, according to Türkiye Today. 'There was a deal... But a substantial part of it was not implemented. Do you see any change in the West's position? I don't,' Grushko told reporters in Vladivostok.

The comments come as Turkey works to reopen a channel for grain shipments. Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said Monday that Ankara had prepared a plan for safe passage and was communicating with both Moscow and Kyiv. The Black Sea was the main subject of Erdogan's 90-minute meeting with Putin on the SCO sidelines in Bishkek, though no breakthrough was announced. Russia's position indicates Moscow does not want to simply restore the previous framework, which enabled nearly 33 million metric tons of Ukrainian grain to reach international markets before Moscow withdrew.
sections.whyItMatters: Russia's refusal to revive the old framework complicates Turkey's mediation effort, which now depends on designing a new arrangement acceptable to Moscow — a harder task given Russia's battlefield confidence and stated unwillingness to negotiate with Ukraine's current leadership.

sections.heading: Kyrenia Ferry Disaster: Second Rescue Vessel Arrives, 20 Still Missing
sections.body:
A second rescue vessel, the TCG Alemdar, arrived off Kyrenia on Wednesday to aid recovery of the passenger ferry that capsized en route to Turkey on Sunday, Cyprus Mail reports. The wreck was located at a depth of 550 meters by the TCG Isin, which arrived Tuesday. Eight people have been confirmed dead and 20 remain missing three days after the disaster.

The recovery effort has taken on a political dimension. Turkish opposition New Party deputy leader Ali Mahir Basarir said Wednesday that 'every single survivor' he met said the captain refused to turn the ferry back to port as conditions deteriorated. Questions have also been raised over the captain's license and the boat's safety certificate. Turkish Cypriot leader Tufan Erhurman confirmed the sunken ship's location Tuesday evening, and officials visited families of the missing on Wednesday morning.
sections.whyItMatters: The disaster has become a test of accountability for both Ankara and the Turkish Cypriot administration, with survivor accounts and questions over the captain's conduct fueling public anger and scrutiny of maritime safety standards.

bottomLine: Turkey's most concrete development today was the defense industry MoU with Egypt in Sarajevo — a step that deepens the Ankara-Cairo rapprochement while Cairo keeps its distance from the Mecca Pact's binding collective-defense clause. On the economic front, a $75 billion hot-money boom into lira assets has stabilized the currency enough for Turkey to repay $5 billion to Saudi Arabia, but leaves policymakers weighing how to manage speculative inflows. Erdogan sharpened his warnings to Greece over Aegean militarization, the Israel-Turkey deconfliction mechanism in Syria remains broken, and Russia's refusal to revive the old Black Sea grain deal complicates Ankara's mediation push. The ferry disaster off Kyrenia continues to generate political fallout over accountability.
sources: Al Bawaba, Middle East Monitor, Bloomberg, MSN Economics, Greek City Times, Ynet, i24NEWS, Middle East Institute (Charles Lister), Türkiye Today, Cyprus Mail, Reuters
